card.summary: A single‑story, 991 cm × 671 cm cottage with a pointed gable roof, red front door, three rooms, a bathroom, and a full‑width porch.
card.description: The modest cottage occupies a tidy 991 cm × 671 cm footprint, its single‑story volume capped by a sharply pointed gable roof of classic asphalt shingles that draws the eye upward. Warm wood siding, painted a neutral cream, frames the façade, while a bold red front door, 90 cm wide and 210 cm tall, provides a welcoming accent that contrasts delightfully with the modest scale. Inside, three well‑proportioned rooms—living, kitchen, and a private bedroom—are arranged around a central hallway, each served by timber‑stud partitions and finished with pine hardwood flooring. A compact bathroom with a standard toilet and sink occupies the rear corner. A 200 cm deep front porch runs the full width of the house, its own gabled roof echoing the main roofline and offering a sheltered space for seasonal sitting. The structure rests on a 15 cm thick concrete slab, supporting timber joists and a robust roof‑truss system that delivers the crisp, pointy silhouette typical of early‑20th‑century bungalow designs. All windows are operable slides, and the interior is wired for basic lighting and a single thermostat, delivering functional comfort within a charming, historically resonant envelope.

White‑painted wood‑frame walls enclose a front porch of 300 cm × 200 cm, its decking of weather‑resistant timber supporting a miniature shingled overhang that mirrors the main roof. A vivid red wooden door, hinged on the north façade, welcomes guests into a bright living room where a sleek flat‑screen TV is mounted on the east wall and a plush fuzzy blue rug anchors the seating area. Two bedrooms and a single bathroom are arranged along the west side, each window sliding on a timber frame to admit daylight. The interior is finished with smooth gypsum drywall and a light‑colored hardwood floor that flows seamlessly from the porch. All structural members – concrete slab, timber studs, and gable trusses – are sized to meet 1920s pattern‑book proportions while integrating modern electrical, plumbing, and HVAC systems. The house reads as a contemporary reinterpretation of the classic Mineola bungalow, retaining its charming porch and efficient layout while adding a pop of red and a splash of blue for personality.

A flat‑screen TV is mounted on the north wall, completing the modern comforts while respecting the historic proportions. Brick exterior walls, timber joists, and drywall ceilings are all detailed to LOD‑300 for precise fabrication, and the entire assembly is documented to LOD‑500 as‑built. A gabled roof of timber trusses carries plywood sheathing and classic asphalt shingles, while a modest front porch of treated lumber and wooden railing greets the solid wood entry door with brass hinges. Double‑hung windows punctuate the north and south elevations, and a two‑car steel garage door occupies the east side. Inside, drywall partitions define a living room, a bedroom, and a compact bathroom equipped with a vanity, toilet, and bathtub. Oak hardwood floors flow beneath a wall‑mounted mirror—90 cm wide, 130 cm tall, and 2 cm deep—situated on the living‑room wall, providing a reflective focal point. The house is fully serviced with electrical conduit, PVC plumbing risers, and a modest kitchen of painted‑wood base cabinets. All components respect the overall envelope, with the largest single element (the foundation slab) occupying roughly one‑third of the building footprint, ensuring structural coherence and ease of BIM replication.
